title: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
summary: Why Windows trusts drivers, how signing works and why it is not enough, how attackers bring vulnerable signed drivers, and the defences: blocklist, App Control, HVCI, KDP, PatchGuard and detection.
outcomes: Explain why signing, not privilege, gates kernel code on Windows, and why admin-to-kernel is not a serviced boundary.
Trace an IOCTL from DeviceIoControl to a driver's dispatch routine and decode its access and method bits.
Explain BYOVD from public advisories, and why a valid signature does not make a driver safe to load.
Review a driver handler for missing access checks and unconstrained operations, and describe the fix.
Deploy and verify the driver blocklist, App Control driver rules, memory integrity and the ASR rule, audit first.
Explain what VBS, HVCI, KDP and PatchGuard each protect and what each leaves open.
Detect suspicious driver loads with Sysmon 6, CodeIntegrity events and Sigma, and triage a BYOVD alert.

lessons.title: Why Windows trusts drivers: the kernel line and the admin line

blocks.md:
**Plain idea.** A fan-control app wants to change how fast a laptop fan spins. The fan is set through a hardware register that only kernel-mode code may touch, so the vendor ships a small **driver**: a module that Windows loads into the kernel and that then runs with the kernel's full power. From the prereq course *How EDR works*, recall the two modes: **user mode**, where programs run in their own address spaces, and **kernel mode**, where the Windows kernel and drivers share one address space and full access to the machine. From *OS security, privilege and isolation*, recall that the boundary between them is enforced by the CPU and crossed only through defined doors such as system calls.

So a driver is not a program the kernel watches. It *is* part of the kernel. Any bug in it, or any feature it exposes carelessly, is a bug or feature of the whole operating system.

**Two different lines.** Microsoft publishes the *Windows security servicing criteria*, the list of boundaries it promises to fix with security updates. One of them is the **kernel boundary**: "A non-administrative user mode process cannot access or tamper with kernel code and data." The same page also says: "For the NT kernel only, Administrator-to-kernel is not a security boundary," because "Administrative processes and users are considered part of the Trusted Computing Base (TCB) for Windows." The **TCB** (trusted computing base) is the set of components the system's security depends on.

That is why an administrator can install a driver at all. Windows does not ask *who* is loading kernel code to decide whether it is safe; it asks *which code* it is, by checking the driver's **digital signature**. Signing is the gate for kernel code. Privilege decides who may open the gate.

blocks.title: Two lines: who may load kernel code, and which code

scenes.caption: A standard user's app runs in user mode. It cannot load a driver or touch kernel memory: that is the kernel boundary Microsoft services.
An administrator is part of the TCB. Windows lets an admin install a driver service; the only remaining question is whether the driver file is signed in a way code integrity accepts.
Code integrity (CI) checks the signature and the driver is mapped into kernel memory. From now on it runs with the same power as the kernel itself.
Apps reach the driver through the I/O manager. Whatever the driver agrees to do for a caller, it does with kernel privilege, including touching hardware.

blocks.code:
# Read-only inventory on a lab Windows machine (elevated PowerShell).
# Every kernel driver Windows knows about, whether it is running, and where it lives.
Get-CimInstance Win32_SystemDriver |
  Select-Object Name, State, StartMode, PathName |
  Sort-Object State, Name

# The same list from the built-in tool, with file paths and link dates
driverquery /v /fo csv | ConvertFrom-Csv | Select-Object 'Module Name', State, Path
blocks.caption: A driver inventory is the first defensive habit: you cannot spot an unusual driver if you do not know the usual ones. Run it on a lab machine; output depends on the machine, so none is shown here.

blocks.md: Two separate questions decide whether kernel code runs: *who* asks (only admins may load drivers, and admin-to-kernel is not a serviced boundary) and *which code* it is (the signature check). Every defence in this course strengthens the second question, because on Windows the first one is already answered once an attacker is admin.

blocks.question: An attacker has a standard user account on a laptop and finds a local bug that lets them write kernel memory. Under Microsoft's servicing criteria, what is this?
options: Not a vulnerability, because admin-to-kernel is not a boundary
A break of the kernel boundary, which Microsoft intends to fix with a security update
Expected behaviour, because drivers share the kernel's address space
Only a problem if memory integrity is turned off
blocks.explain: The serviced kernel boundary says a non-administrative user mode process cannot access or tamper with kernel code and data. A standard user reaching kernel memory breaks it. The admin-to-kernel exception applies only when the caller is already an administrator.

blocks.question: Why does Windows rely on driver signatures rather than on the caller's privilege to keep bad code out of the kernel?
options: Because standard users can load drivers
Because signatures also prove the driver has no bugs
Because administrators are treated as part of the TCB, so privilege cannot separate safe from unsafe kernel code
Because signing is faster than an access check
blocks.explain: Admins are trusted by design, so checking privilege cannot tell a good driver from a bad one: any admin may load either. The signature tells Windows who built the file and that it was not changed. As later lessons show, it says nothing about whether the code is safe.

lessons.title: How programs talk to drivers: device objects, IRPs and IOCTLs

blocks.md: **Plain idea.** The fan app cannot call a function inside the driver directly; kernel code lives behind the boundary. Instead it opens a named object that the driver created, and sends it numbered requests. Tiny example: the app opens `\\.\ToyFan` and asks for request number `0x80016000`, meaning "read the fan speed". **ToyFan** is a made-up driver from Fabrikam, the fictional company Microsoft uses in its own documentation; we use it throughout this course.

Three terms, each defined once:
- A **device object** is the kernel object a driver creates to receive requests. It has a name such as `\Device\ToyFan`, a symbolic link that user mode can open, and a **security descriptor** that says who may open it (the access check from *Windows for security*).
- An **IRP** (I/O request packet) is the structure the **I/O manager**, the part of the kernel that routes I/O, builds for every request and hands to the driver.
- An **IOCTL** (input/output control) is a 32-bit request code for device-specific operations, sent by user mode with `DeviceIoControl` and delivered to the driver as an `IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL` request.

blocks.title: One IOCTL from an app to ToyFan and back

scenes.caption: The app opens the device. The I/O manager runs the normal access check: the caller's token against the device object's security descriptor. Only then does the app get a handle.
The app sends IOCTL 0x80016000. Its Access bits say READ_DATA, and this handle was granted read, so the I/O manager builds an IRP and calls the driver's dispatch routine.
The driver reads the hardware register, copies the answer into the system buffer and completes the IRP. Everything the driver did ran in kernel mode.
A request whose Access bits demand WRITE_DATA is refused by the I/O manager for this read-only handle. The driver never sees it. This check works only if the driver declared the right bits.

blocks.md:
**Inside the 32-bit code.** Microsoft's *Defining I/O Control Codes* page gives the layout, built by the `CTL_CODE` macro as `(DeviceType << 16) | (Access << 14) | (Function << 2) | Method`:
- **DeviceType** (bits 16 to 30) and the *Common* bit (31): vendors use 0x8000 to 0xFFFF, so the top bit of their value lands in bit 31 and sets Common.
- **Access** (bits 14 and 15): `FILE_ANY_ACCESS` (0), `FILE_READ_DATA` (1), `FILE_WRITE_DATA` (2) or both. "The I/O manager will create IRPs and call the driver with a particular IOCTL only if the caller requested the specified access rights."
- **Function** (bits 2 to 12): vendors use 0x800 to 0xFFF, which sets bit 13, the *Custom* bit.
- **Method** (bits 0 and 1): how buffers travel. `METHOD_BUFFERED` (0) copies data through a kernel buffer; `METHOD_IN_DIRECT` and `METHOD_OUT_DIRECT` (1, 2) lock the caller's pages; `METHOD_NEITHER` (3) hands the driver raw user-mode addresses "without validating or mapping them".

scenes.caption: The six fields of an IOCTL, high bits on the left. Common and Custom are single bits that mark vendor-defined values.
DeviceType 0x8001 is in the vendor range, so its top bit (the Common bit) is 1. Function 0x801 is in the vendor range, so the Custom bit is 1.
Access 2 means FILE_WRITE_DATA: the I/O manager delivers this IOCTL only on a handle opened with write access. Method 0 is METHOD_BUFFERED, the safest default.
If the vendor had written FILE_ANY_ACCESS (0) here, any process holding any handle to the device could send it. The bit is the vendor's choice, not Windows'.

blocks.caption: Build and decode ToyFan's two IOCTLs with the CTL_CODE formula. Run it with python3; the output is real.

blocks.prompt: ToyFan's device object has a security descriptor that lets every user open it for reading. Its GET_SPEED IOCTL is declared READ_DATA and its SET_SPEED IOCTL WRITE_DATA. A standard user opens the device with read access. Which requests reach the driver?
blocks.reveal: Only GET_SPEED. The open succeeds (the ACL grants read), and the I/O manager compares each IOCTL's Access bits with the access granted on the handle. SET_SPEED needs write, so it is rejected before the driver runs. Two checks cooperate: the device ACL (who may open) and the Access bits (what each handle may ask). A driver that declares FILE_ANY_ACCESS throws away the second check.

blocks.question: Which IOCTL transfer method gives a driver the caller's raw user-mode buffer addresses without any validation by the I/O manager?
options: METHOD_BUFFERED
METHOD_IN_DIRECT
METHOD_OUT_DIRECT
METHOD_NEITHER
blocks.explain: With METHOD_NEITHER, the IRP carries the user-mode virtual addresses as given to DeviceIoControl, unvalidated and unmapped. The driver must probe them and wrap every access in an exception handler. Buffered I/O copies through a kernel buffer; direct I/O locks the pages and maps them with an MDL (memory descriptor list).

blocks.question: An IOCTL code ends in the two bits 00 and has Access bits 00. What does that tell you?
options: It is buffered and any handle may send it
It is direct I/O and needs admin rights
It is METHOD_NEITHER and read-only
It is reserved for Microsoft
blocks.explain: Method 0 is METHOD_BUFFERED and Access 0 is FILE_ANY_ACCESS, so any process with any handle to the device can send it. Whether that is dangerous depends on what the handler does, which is the subject of the BYOVD lessons.

lessons.title: Driver signing: from cross-signing to Microsoft's portal

blocks.md:
**Plain idea.** A signature on a driver is like a sealed envelope with a return address: it proves who sent the file and that nobody changed it on the way. Windows uses **Authenticode**, Microsoft's code-signing format for PE (Portable Executable) files such as `.sys` drivers. You met module signing for Linux in *OS security, privilege and isolation*; Windows applies the same idea, with Microsoft deciding whose signatures the kernel accepts.

The rules changed three times, and old rules leave old drivers behind, which is the root of BYOVD.

**Era 1: cross-signing.** From Windows Vista, 64-bit Windows refused unsigned kernel drivers (Microsoft's signing table: "64-bit only, no signature required for 32-bit" on Vista and 7). A vendor bought a code-signing certificate from a commercial certificate authority (CA) and signed together with a **cross-certificate**: a certificate Microsoft issued to that CA so its chain led to a root the kernel trusted. The kernel trusted the vendor's own signature, with no Microsoft review of the driver.

**Era 2: Microsoft signs everything new.** "Starting with Windows 10, version 1607, Windows will not load any new kernel-mode drivers which are not signed by the Dev Portal" (the Windows Hardware Dev Center). Three exceptions kept cross-signed drivers loading: the PC was upgraded from an earlier release, Secure Boot is off, or the driver "was signed with an end-entity certificate issued prior to July 29th 2015 that chains to a supported cross-signed CA." Most cross-certificates then expired in July 2021, and Microsoft now states that "all cross-signed trusted root certificates are now expired."

**The three ways Microsoft signs a driver today** (*Driver Signing Options* page):
- **HLK-tested (WHCP) signing.** The vendor runs the **HLK** (Hardware Lab Kit) test suite and submits the logs. **WHCP** is the Windows Hardware Compatibility Program, formerly **WHQL** (Windows Hardware Quality Labs). It "works on Windows Vista and later, including Windows Server editions" and is what Windows Update distributes to retail users.
- **Attestation signing.** The vendor signs a package with an **EV** (extended validation) certificate, whose issuer verified the company's identity more strictly, and Microsoft re-signs it without HLK testing. Microsoft is blunt: an attestation signature "indicates that Windows trusts the driver. But because the driver isn't tested in HLK Studio, there are no assurances about compatibility or functionality." It works only on Windows 10 desktop and later, and is now described as for testing scenarios.
- **Test signing.** For development only, with the `TESTSIGNING` boot option enabled on the test machine.

blocks.title: Which driver signatures the kernel accepted, 2007 to 2026

scenes.caption: Years are counted from 2007 (Windows Vista). In the cross-signing era any vendor with a commercial certificate and a cross-certificate could sign kernel drivers itself.
Windows 10 version 1607 (2016): new drivers must be signed by Microsoft's Dev Center, after HLK testing or by attestation.
But the exceptions kept older cross-signed drivers loading: leaf certificates issued before 29 July 2015, upgraded PCs, Secure Boot off. A 2013 utility driver still loads.
July 2021: most cross-certificates expire, so nobody can make new cross-signed kernel signatures. Drivers timestamped before expiry keep working.
April 2026: Windows 11 24H2 and later and Server 2025 start removing default trust for the cross-signed program altogether (next lesson).

blocks.caption: A toy model of the rules above. Simplified: real code integrity also checks hashes, revocation, policy and more, and Microsoft's signing-options table marks drivers cross-signed with SHA-1 certificates as not accepted on Windows 10 from version 1809.

blocks.code:
== win10, Secure Boot on
  newfan.sys   LOAD  signed by Microsoft (Dev Center)
  labtool.sys  LOAD  signed by Microsoft (Dev Center)
  oldutil.sys  LOAD  cross-signed exception applies
  late.sys     BLOCK cross-signed, leaf after cutoff, Secure Boot on
== win10, Secure Boot off
  newfan.sys   LOAD  signed by Microsoft (Dev Center)
  labtool.sys  LOAD  signed by Microsoft (Dev Center)
  oldutil.sys  LOAD  cross-signed exception applies
  late.sys     LOAD  cross-signed exception applies
== win11 24H2, enforced
  newfan.sys   LOAD  signed by Microsoft (Dev Center)
  labtool.sys  LOAD  signed by Microsoft (Dev Center)
  oldutil.sys  BLOCK 2026 policy: cross-signed, not allow-listed
  late.sys     BLOCK 2026 policy: cross-signed, not allow-listed
blocks.caption: Output of the script above (run with Python 3).

blocks.md: Misconception: "since 2016 only Microsoft-signed drivers load." Only *new* drivers had to go through Microsoft. Drivers already signed under the cross-signing program, with leaf certificates from before 29 July 2015, kept loading on most systems for a decade. Many drivers later abused in BYOVD attacks date from that era.

blocks.question: A vendor wants a new kernel driver to reach retail users through Windows Update on Windows 11 and Windows Server 2025. Which signing route fits?
options: HLK testing and WHCP (dashboard) signing
Attestation signing with an EV certificate
Cross-signing with a commercial CA certificate
Test signing with the TESTSIGNING boot option
blocks.explain: Attestation-signed drivers cannot be published to Windows Update for retail audiences and do not load on Windows Server 2016 and later. Cross-signing is no longer accepted, and test signing is for development machines. HLK-tested WHCP signing covers client and Server.

blocks.question: Microsoft attestation-signs a driver. What does that signature promise?
options: That Microsoft tested the driver for security bugs
That the driver passed the Hardware Lab Kit
That Windows trusts the publisher's identity and the file is unchanged, with no assurance about how the code behaves
That the driver is compatible with memory integrity
blocks.explain: Microsoft says attestation means Windows trusts the driver, but because it was not HLK-tested there are no assurances about compatibility or functionality. A signature binds a file to a vetted identity; it is not a code review.

lessons.title: What a signature proves, revocation, and the 2026 trust change

blocks.md:
**Plain idea.** A signature answers "who made this file, and is it unchanged?" It does not answer "is this code safe to run in the kernel?" Tiny example: in 2013 Fabrikam signs `oldutil.sys`, a fan utility driver with a careless IOCTL. Ten years later the bug is public. The signature is still mathematically valid, the certificate was valid when the file was timestamped, and Microsoft's deprecation page confirms that packages "timestamped before the expiration date of the leaf-signing certificate" keep working. Nothing about the signature changed when the world learned the code was dangerous.

So Windows needs a second mechanism that can say "this signed file, no more". There are two:
- **Revocation** of the certificate, which kills every file it signed. Logged as event 3033 (often a revoked signature), 3036 ("Microsoft or the certificate issuing authority revoked the certificate"), 3112 ("Windows has revoked the certificate").
- **Deny rules** for specific files or versions while the publisher's other drivers stay trusted. That is the vulnerable driver blocklist of lesson 10.

**The 2026 change.** On 26 March 2026, Microsoft's Peter Waxman announced in the Windows IT Pro blog "the removal of trust for all kernel drivers signed by the deprecated cross-signed root program." The reasons given: the program dates to the early 2000s, its certificates came with varying vetting and no assurance of security, and it relied on publishers protecting private keys, "which led to abuse and credential theft". The program was deprecated in 2021, but trust "has persisted in specific use cases and scenarios".

What changed, from the post and Microsoft's support article *The Windows Driver Policy*:
- Scope: Windows 11 24H2, 25H2 and 26H1 and Windows Server 2025, from the April 2026 update, and all future versions.
- An **evaluation mode** first audits driver loads without blocking. Enforcement starts only after 250 hours of uptime (raised from 100 in June 2026) and 3 restarts (2 on Server 2025) without a violation; a violation resets the counters.
- Microsoft keeps an explicit **allow list** of widely used cross-signed drivers. Other drivers that are neither WHCP-signed nor allow-listed are blocked.
- Organisations can allow their own signers with an App Control policy signed by an authority in the device's Secure Boot PK or KEK (platform key or key exchange key, the top Secure Boot keys in UEFI firmware; whoever holds them decides what the firmware trusts).
- An administrator can turn the policy off (after the July 2026 update, with only a restart). A BYOVD attacker is an admin too, so check that the enforce policy is still listed by `citool -lp`.

blocks.title: The 2026 kernel trust policy on one PC

scenes.caption: The April 2026 update installs the policy in evaluation mode. Drivers that would be blocked are audited (event 3076) but still load.
Each clean period counts towards 250 hours of uptime and 3 restarts. An old cross-signed driver that is not allow-listed loads and is audited.
That audited load is a violation: the counters go back to zero and the PC stays in evaluation. It will never enforce while that driver keeps loading.
Once the driver is replaced with a WHCP-signed version (or removed) and the counters complete, enforcement starts. Disallowed drivers now fail with event 3077.

blocks.code:
# Read-only checks on a lab Windows 11 machine (elevated PowerShell).

# 1. Does a driver's chain end in an expired cross-signing root?
#    Microsoft: if the chain ends in 'Microsoft Code Verification Root',
#    the signature came from the cross-signing program.
signtool verify /v /kp C:\Lab\oldutil.sys

# 2. Which code integrity policies are active, and in which mode?
#    The support article says to check IsEnforced and IsAuthorized for the
#    Windows Driver Policy GUIDs: audit {784C4414-...} and enforce {8F9CB695-...}.
citool -lp -json

# 3. What would have been blocked (3076) or was blocked (3077) in the last day?
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational';
  Id=3076,3077; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddDays(-1)} | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, Message
blocks.caption: signtool comes with the Windows SDK and WDK; citool is built into recent Windows. Run on a lab machine; output not shown because it depends on the machine.

blocks.prompt: A Windows 11 25H2 laptop has been running for months, yet `citool` shows the Windows Driver Policy still in audit mode. The CodeIntegrity log shows a 3076 event for the same driver after every boot. What is going on?
blocks.reveal: The laptop is stuck in evaluation mode. Each boot loads a cross-signed driver that is neither WHCP-signed nor on Microsoft's allow list, which counts as a violation and resets the 250-hour and restart counters. Enforcement will never begin until that driver is updated to a WHCP-signed version or removed. The 3076 event names the driver and the process that loaded it, so it tells you exactly what to chase.

blocks.md: A signature is about identity and integrity, never about behaviour. Old, validly signed drivers stay valid forever unless something revokes them, denies them by rule, or (since 2026) removes trust from their whole signing program.

blocks.question: Why can't Microsoft simply revoke the certificate of every vendor that once shipped a vulnerable driver?
options: Revocation is not supported for kernel drivers
Revoking a certificate kills every file it signed, including the vendor's fixed and unrelated drivers, which could break hardware
Revoked certificates still load if Secure Boot is on
Only the vendor can revoke its own certificate
blocks.explain: Revocation works at the certificate level, so it blocks all files signed with that certificate. For a malicious signer that is the goal (as in ADV220005, lesson 9). For an honest vendor with one bad driver, deny rules for that file and its vulnerable versions are far less disruptive.

blocks.question: Under the 2026 kernel trust policy, how can an organisation keep loading its own internal, cross-signed driver?
options: Turn off Secure Boot
Add the driver's hash to the Sysmon configuration
Set the driver's service Start value to 0
Deploy an App Control policy that allows that signer, signed by an authority in the device's Secure Boot PK or KEK
blocks.explain: Microsoft's post says customers can allow custom signers through an App Control for Business policy signed by an authority in the Secure Boot PK or KEK variables, which requires controlling those UEFI authorities. Sysmon only logs; it never decides what loads.

lessons.title: BYOVD: a signed driver with a dangerous interface

blocks.md:
**Plain idea.** An attacker who already has admin rights on a host wants to switch off the EDR sensor, whose processes are protected and whose callbacks live in the kernel. Loading their own unsigned driver fails. So they **bring their own vulnerable driver**: a legitimately signed, often old, third-party driver whose IOCTL lets a caller ask it to do something powerful, and they use it as a tool. MITRE ATT&CK describes it under Exploitation for Privilege Escalation ([T1068](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1068/)): "Adversaries may bring a signed vulnerable driver onto a compromised machine so that they can exploit the vulnerability to execute code in kernel mode. This process is sometimes referred to as Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD)."

You met the idea in *How EDR works* (the AuKill case, which abused an old Microsoft-signed Process Explorer driver). Here we look at why it works and what the defences target.

MITRE's weakness catalogue names the root bug [CWE-782](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/782.html): *Exposed IOCTL with Insufficient Access Control*. Such drivers usually were not written by attackers. They come from overclocking tools, hardware monitors and firmware updaters: software-only utilities that need one narrow hardware capability and expose a general one. From *OS security, privilege and isolation*, this is a **confused deputy**: a privileged component doing a request for a less trusted caller without asking whether that caller should be allowed.

blocks.title: A BYOVD attack, and where each defence sits

nodes.label:
Old signed driver
written to disk

scenes.caption: Start: the attacker already has admin rights (stolen credentials, an exploit). Every BYOVD needs this first step; keeping admin rare is the first defence.
They write an old, validly signed driver to disk and create a kernel driver service for it.
Code integrity checks the signature. It is valid, so without a deny rule the driver loads. Signing did its job: this file really is the vendor's.
The attacker opens the device and sends IOCTLs. The driver, acting as a confused deputy, performs privileged operations: stopping protected processes or changing kernel data.

Defences map to steps: ASR rule at the disk write, blocklist and App Control at the load, HVCI (memory integrity) and KDP (Kernel Data Protection, lesson 13) limit what kernel writes can change, and every step leaves telemetry.

blocks.md:
**Why it keeps working.**
1. **Admin-to-kernel is not a boundary** (lesson 1), so loading a driver is an admin's right.
2. **Signatures never expire in practice**: timestamped signatures stay valid, and old cross-signed drivers loaded on most systems until 2026 (lessons 3 and 4).
3. **The flaw is in the interface, not the signature.** The driver does what it was built to do, for anyone who asks.
4. **Supply is large.** Researchers keep finding such drivers: the POPKORN study (presented at ACSAC 2022, the Annual Computer Security Applications Conference) analysed 212 signed drivers and reported 38 high-impact bugs in 27 of them (lesson 7).

**What attackers do with it**, at the level of public advisories: terminate protected security processes (AuKill), remove the kernel callbacks EDR sensors rely on (BlackByte, lesson 8), switch off security monitoring (Lazarus, lesson 8), or tamper with code integrity policy so that unsigned code loads. Microsoft's 2020 Kernel Data Protection announcement reports seeing attackers use signed but vulnerable drivers to attack policy data structures.

blocks.code:
# Review made-up driver interfaces against Microsoft's list of unsafe
# behaviours (arbitrary MSR, port I/O, memory access, process termination).
UNSAFE = {"msr_rw", "port_io", "mem_rw", "phys_map", "kill_process"}

drivers = {
    "toyfan.sys":  [("SET_REG", "msr_rw", "ANY_ACCESS", "unconstrained"),
                    ("GET_SPEED", "read_sensor", "READ_DATA", "fixed")],
    "camlight.sys": [("LED_ON", "device_io", "WRITE_DATA", "fixed")],
    "updater.sys": [("COPY", "mem_rw", "WRITE_DATA", "unconstrained"),
                    ("STOP", "kill_process", "WRITE_DATA", "checks PPL")],
}
for drv, ioctls in drivers.items():
    findings = []
    for name, op, access, limits in ioctls:
        if op in UNSAFE and limits == "unconstrained":
            sev = "HIGH" if access == "ANY_ACCESS" else "HIGH (admins can still abuse it)"
            findings.append(f"{name}: {op} {limits}, {access}: {sev}")
    print(drv, "|", "; ".join(findings) or "no unsafe operation exposed")

# Output:
# toyfan.sys | SET_REG: msr_rw unconstrained, ANY_ACCESS: HIGH
# camlight.sys | no unsafe operation exposed
# updater.sys | COPY: mem_rw unconstrained, WRITE_DATA: HIGH (admins can still abuse it)
blocks.caption: Reviewing driver interfaces the way a defender or vendor security team would: list each IOCTL's operation, its Access bits and its limits, and flag unconstrained unsafe operations. All drivers here are made up.

blocks.md: Misconception: "we only allow signed drivers, so kernel malware is handled." Requiring signatures stops *unsigned* code. BYOVD uses *signed* code that is dangerous by design or by bug. You need a second layer that can refuse specific signed files: the blocklist, App Control deny rules, or the 2026 cross-signed trust removal.

blocks.question: Which statement best explains why BYOVD needs admin rights first, even when the vulnerable IOCTL is declared FILE_ANY_ACCESS?
options: Because IOCTLs only work for admins
Because code integrity checks the caller's token
Because loading a driver (installing the service) is an administrator action, so the attacker must be admin to get the driver into the kernel at all
Because FILE_ANY_ACCESS means administrators only
blocks.explain: If the vulnerable driver is already installed and its device is open to everyone, a standard user could abuse it, which is a privilege escalation. In BYOVD the attacker brings the driver, and creating a kernel driver service needs admin rights. FILE_ANY_ACCESS means any handle, not admin only.

blocks.question: A security team lists drivers to review first. Which made-up driver should top the list?
options: A software-only utility driver whose IOCTL copies memory between caller-chosen addresses
A WHCP-signed network driver with buffered IOCTLs that validate lengths
A signed camera driver whose only IOCTL turns an LED on, declared WRITE_DATA
An unsigned test driver on a build server with test signing off
blocks.explain: Arbitrary memory read or write is on Microsoft's list of unsafe behaviours and is the classic BYOVD capability. A software-only driver also loads on any PC. The unsigned driver cannot load with test signing off, and the other two expose narrow, fixed operations.

lessons.title: Inside a vulnerable IOCTL handler, and the fix

blocks.md:
**Plain idea.** ToyFan v1 lets the fan app set the fan speed by writing a CPU register. The developer made it general: the caller names *which* register and *what* value. That one shortcut turns a fan utility into a tool that can rewrite any CPU configuration register for anyone who can open the device. This lesson reads the vulnerable handler, animates what goes wrong, and fixes it in four steps. ToyFan is made up; the pattern is the one Microsoft describes in its best-practices page, where an unconstrained `__writemsr` "can result in abuse by malicious processes to elevate privilege".

Two terms: a **dispatch routine** is the driver function the I/O manager calls for one kind of IRP, here `IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL`. **SDDL** (Security Descriptor Definition Language) is Windows' text format for a security descriptor, such as `D:P(A;;GA;;;SY)(A;;GA;;;BA)`, which means: a protected DACL (`D:P`) allowing (`A`) all access (`GA`, generic all) to SYSTEM (`SY`) and to built-in Administrators (`BA`).

blocks.caption: Pseudocode in C for a made-up driver, written to show the bug. It is not a real product and not meant to be built.

blocks.title: ToyFan v1 handling two requests

scenes.caption: The fan app sends SET_REG with the fan's register and a speed. Nothing is checked, and this time nothing goes wrong: the caller happened to be honest.
The write happens with kernel privilege. The driver trusts the register number because the developer assumed only the fan app would call.
Any other process can open the device: v1's SDDL admits Everyone, and FILE_ANY_ACCESS lets every handle send the IOCTL. It names a different register.
Same line, same privilege, but now the kernel writes a CPU configuration register the vendor never meant to expose. The driver has become a confused deputy.
scenes.output: CPU configuration changed on behalf of an untrusted caller

scenes.caption: Also missing: the handler reads req before checking InputBufferLength, so a short buffer makes it read past the data the caller sent.

blocks.caption: The fix, also pseudocode for the made-up driver. Each numbered comment closes one gap; IoCreateDeviceSecure, FILE_DEVICE_SECURE_OPEN, the SDDL string and CTL_CODE are documented names from the WDK (Windows Driver Kit).

blocks.md:
**Why each step works.**
1. **The device ACL.** Microsoft's checklist says to secure named device objects with `IoCreateDeviceSecure` and an SDDL string (with a custom class GUID). `SDDL_DEVOBJ_SYS_ALL_ADM_ALL`, the string above, "allows the kernel, system, and administrator complete control over the device. No other users may access the device." Without `FILE_DEVICE_SECURE_OPEN`, opens of names *below* the device, such as `\Device\ToyFan\x`, are not checked against the device ACL at all and are left to the driver.
2. **The Access bits.** `FILE_WRITE_DATA` makes the I/O manager refuse the IOCTL on handles without write access. Microsoft's rule: "Always specify a RequiredAccess value." Drivers can call `IoValidateDeviceIoControlAccess` for stricter checks.
3. **The length check.** "Never read or write more data than the buffer ... can contain"; check `InputBufferLength` first.
4. **The constraint.** The caller no longer chooses the register, and the value is bounded. This is the step that matters against BYOVD, because steps 1 and 2 do not stop an attacker who is already admin.

blocks.code:
# Simulation of a made-up driver, ToyFan, before and after its fix.
# The "kernel" is a dict of registers; only FAN_REG is meant to be touched.
FAN_REG = 0x40
kernel = {0x40: 1200, 0x41: 0, 0x7F: 1}        # 0x7F: a made-up protection flag

def open_device(caller, sddl_admins_only):
    if sddl_admins_only and caller != "admin":
        return None                              # I/O manager denies the open
    return {"caller": caller, "granted": {"read", "write"} if caller == "admin" else {"read"}}

def set_reg_v1(handle, reg, value):              # IOCTL declared FILE_ANY_ACCESS
    kernel[reg] = value                          # no range check at all
    return "ok"

def set_reg_v2(handle, reg, value):              # IOCTL declared FILE_WRITE_DATA
    if "write" not in handle["granted"]:
        return "STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED"            # I/O manager check
    if reg != FAN_REG or not 0 <= value <= 3000:
        return "STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER"        # handler constrains its input
    kernel[reg] = value
    return "ok"

h = open_device("user", sddl_admins_only=False)
print("v1 user writes 0x7F:", set_reg_v1(h, 0x7F, 0), kernel[0x7F])
kernel[0x7F] = 1
print("v2 user open:", open_device("user", sddl_admins_only=True))
h = open_device("admin", sddl_admins_only=True)
print("v2 admin writes 0x7F:", set_reg_v2(h, 0x7F, 0), kernel[0x7F])
print("v2 admin sets fan:", set_reg_v2(h, FAN_REG, 1800), kernel[FAN_REG])

# Output:
# v1 user writes 0x7F: ok 0
# v2 user open: None
# v2 admin writes 0x7F: STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER 1
# v2 admin sets fan: ok 1800
blocks.caption: A runnable simulation of the two versions. The 'kernel' is a Python dict and the register numbers are made up; the point is which checks stop which caller.

blocks.md: Access control decides *who* may ask; constraints decide *what* can be asked. An admin-only device still makes a perfect BYOVD tool if its handler writes any register or any address. A driver is safe to leave on a machine only when even an administrator cannot use it to do more than its job.

blocks.question: A vendor fixes a driver by changing the device ACL to SYSTEM and Administrators only, but keeps the IOCTL that copies memory between caller-supplied addresses. Is the driver still useful for BYOVD?
options: No, because standard users can no longer open it
Yes, because a BYOVD attacker is already an administrator and the unconstrained copy is still there
No, because FILE_DEVICE_SECURE_OPEN blocks memory copies
Yes, but only if memory integrity is off
blocks.explain: BYOVD starts with admin rights, so an admin-only ACL does not stop it. Only removing or constraining the dangerous operation does. That is why Microsoft's best practices require constraining source and destination to expected ranges, and why WHCP requires new submissions to follow them.

blocks.question: Without FILE_DEVICE_SECURE_OPEN, what happens when a caller opens a name under the device, such as a path below the device name?
options: The open always fails
The device ACL is not checked for that open; security for names in the device's namespace is left to the driver
Windows applies the ACL of the parent directory
The open is converted to a read-only handle
blocks.explain: Microsoft's page on device namespace access says that by default, security checks for file opens within the device's namespace are left entirely to the driver and the device object ACL is not checked. Setting FILE_DEVICE_SECURE_OPEN applies the device's security descriptor to all of them.

lessons.title: Buffers, double fetches and Microsoft's driver security checklist

blocks.md: **Plain idea.** Even a driver with a narrow, well-protected interface can be broken by the *data* it receives. Tiny example: a logging IOCTL accepts a message and its length. If the driver checks the length, then reads it again from user memory to do the copy, another thread of the same caller can change the number in between. You met this pattern as TOCTOU (time of check to time of use) in *OS security, privilege and isolation*, and the overflow it leads to in *Memory safety bugs*. In a driver, the overflow happens in the kernel.

blocks.title: A double fetch: the length changes between check and use

scenes.caption: The driver receives a raw user pointer (METHOD_NEITHER) and probes it. Probing checks the address range is user memory; it does not freeze the contents.
Fetch 1: the driver reads Len from user memory and checks it. 40 is less than 64, so the check passes.
Meanwhile a second thread of the same caller writes 4000 into Len. User memory is still the caller's to change.
Fetch 2: the copy reads Len again and copies 4000 bytes into a 64-byte stack buffer: a kernel stack overflow (Memory safety bugs).
The fix reads Len once into a kernel variable, checks that copy and uses that copy. Thread 2 can change user memory all it likes; the driver never looks again.

blocks.md:
**Microsoft's driver security checklist**, the headline items:
1. Confirm a kernel driver is required; a service or app is lower risk.
2. Use the driver frameworks (KMDF, the Kernel-Mode Driver Framework).
3. Manage access control (SDDL, `IoCreateDeviceSecure`).
4. Restrict **software-only drivers** to the hardware they serve. Microsoft's own example is an OEM overclocking utility, which should check for its hardware, for example in the SMBIOS (System Management BIOS) table, "before enabling any capabilities".
5. Follow secure coding: buffers, TOCTOU, constrained MSR access, NX (non-executable) pool memory.
6. Write HVCI-compatible code (no writable and executable sections).
7. to 10. Secure installation, technology guidance, SAL (source code annotation language) and peer review.
11. to 15. Threat modelling, CodeQL, Driver Verifier, HLK tests, BinSkim (Microsoft's checker for binary security settings) and SignTool.
16. to 19. Never production-sign test code, ship through the portal, know the Vulnerable and Malicious Driver Reporting Center, keep learning.

blocks.title: POPKORN: what an automated driver scan found (ACSAC 2022)

scenes.caption: The researchers ran their tool, which combines taint analysis with targeted symbolic execution, on 212 unique signed Windows kernel drivers.
It reported 38 high-impact bugs across 27 unique drivers, and manual verification found no false positives.
31 of the bugs were previously unknown and could potentially allow elevation of privilege. Signed drivers with such bugs are the raw material of BYOVD.

blocks.md:
The numbers come from the [POPKORN abstract](https://acsac.org/2022/program/final/s91.html) by Rajat Gupta, Lukas Dresel, Noah Spahn, Giovanni Vigna, Christopher Kruegel and Taesoo Kim (Georgia Tech and UC Santa Barbara). Their framing matches this course: vendors write a large share of Windows drivers, "Microsoft relies on these vendors to handle all aspects of driver security", and testing drivers is hard without source code or the physical device.

For a vendor, the practical tools are the ones in the checklist: [CodeQL](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/devtest/static-tools-and-codeql) to find bug patterns in source, and [Driver Verifier](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/devtest/driver-verifier), which monitors kernel-mode and graphics drivers in real time and "detects illegal function calls and problematic actions that could destabilize your system".

Reviewing a driver? Start with three questions: Who can open the device (its SDDL)? Which IOCTLs accept FILE_ANY_ACCESS? Does any handler let the caller choose an address, a register, a port or a process? A yes to the last question is a finding even if the answer to the first is "admins only".

blocks.question: A driver probes a METHOD_NEITHER buffer with ProbeForRead, checks a length field in it, then copies using that field. Why is ProbeForRead not enough?
options: ProbeForRead only works for METHOD_BUFFERED
ProbeForRead must be called after the copy
ProbeForRead locks the buffer, which causes a deadlock
ProbeForRead checks the address range once; the caller can still change the buffer's contents after the check, so the length must be copied into kernel memory first
blocks.explain: Probing validates that the range is user memory with the right access; it does not freeze the data. A second thread can change the length between check and use. Copying the parameter into kernel-only memory, then validating and using that copy, removes the race.

blocks.question: Which checklist item most directly reduces the chance that an overclocking utility's driver becomes a BYOVD tool on PCs from other manufacturers?
options: Restrict software-only drivers to the hardware they serve, for example by checking SMBIOS before enabling capabilities
Add SAL annotations
Use NonPagedPoolNx for allocations
Run BinSkim before release
blocks.explain: Software-only drivers can be loaded on any PC, which is what makes them portable attack tools. Microsoft's checklist says they must verify they run on the intended hardware, using a unique PnP (Plug and Play) ID or an SMBIOS check. The other items improve quality but do not limit where the driver works.

lessons.title: Case files: BlackByte and Lazarus bring their own drivers

blocks.md: **Plain idea.** Two public cases from 2021 and 2022 show the same pattern from different attackers: a criminal ransomware group and a state-linked espionage group each brought a legitimately signed hardware-utility driver to switch off security tools. We study them as advisories and write-ups describe them: the bug class, the timeline, the patch and what defenders could have seen. Neither case needs exploitation details to teach the defence.

**Case 1: Lazarus and a Dell firmware-update driver (2021).** ESET, a Slovak security company, [reported](https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/09/30/amazon-themed-campaigns-lazarus-netherlands-belgium/) on 30 September 2022 that the Lazarus group (also known as HIDDEN COBRA, active since at least 2009) attacked an employee of an aerospace company in the Netherlands and a political journalist in Belgium in autumn 2021. Both received Amazon-themed documents posing as job offers, one through LinkedIn Messaging and one by email; the goal was data theft.

On the Dutch victim's machine the attackers used a tool whose internal name ESET found to be **FudModule**, which abused **CVE-2021-21551** in `dbutil_2_3.sys`, a Dell driver shipped with BIOS and firmware update utilities. ESET says the tool, through the bug, switched off seven mechanisms Windows offers to monitor its activity, and so "disables the monitoring of all security solutions on compromised machines". ESET calls it the "first ever recorded abuse of this vulnerability in the wild".

Dell's advisory DSA-2021-088 (4 May 2021) describes "an insufficient access control vulnerability" that "may lead to escalation of privileges, denial of service, or information disclosure", needing local authenticated access. CISA added it to its [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog) on 31 March 2022, classed as CWE-782, the exposed-IOCTL weakness from lesson 5.

**Case 2: BlackByte and an overclocking driver (2022).** Andreas Klopsch, a threat researcher at Sophos (a British security company), reported in October 2022 that the BlackByte ransomware dropped `RTCore64.sys`, a driver of MSI Afterburner 4.6.2.15658 (a graphics-card overclocking utility from MSI, Micro-Star International), vulnerable as **CVE-2019-16098** ([NVD entry](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2019-16098)). In that Sophos write-up, *BlackByte ransomware returns*, BlackByte used the driver to remove the kernel callbacks that security products register (the notification routines from the *Where a sensor sits* lesson of the EDR course) for any driver on its list of more than 1,000 that security products rely on. The same write-up reports that it also switched off the Microsoft-Windows-Threat-Intelligence ETW provider.

Sophos's advice was defensive and generic: find out which legitimate drivers attackers are currently exploiting and block them, "always keep track of the drivers installed on your systems", and keep systems updated. Microsoft's memory integrity page now notes that the blocklist "can help disrupt techniques used by ransomware such as BlackByte 2.0 when the abused driver is included on the blocklist".

blocks.title: From vendor fix to attacks to defender intelligence, 2021 to 2022

scenes.caption: Months counted from January 2021. CVE-2019-16098 had been public since 2019. Dell publishes DSA-2021-088 and a removal utility in May 2021.
Autumn 2021: Lazarus uses the Dell driver against targets in the Netherlands and Belgium. A patch existed, but nothing stopped the attacker from bringing the old, still validly signed file.
31 March 2022: CISA adds CVE-2021-21551 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, a signal defenders can automate on.
September and October 2022: ESET publishes the Lazarus case and Sophos the BlackByte case. Public detail on the Lazarus attacks arrives about a year after they happened.

blocks.md:
**What would have stopped each, step by step.**
- **Patching was not enough.** Dell fixed its products, but BYOVD attackers bring the *old* file. Dell's own remediation therefore also says to apply Microsoft's recommended driver block rules to stop reinstallation.
- **Block the file at load time.** A blocklist or App Control deny rule covering the vulnerable versions refuses the load even though the signature is valid (lessons 10 and 11). Memory integrity enforces Microsoft's list automatically.
- **Block the write.** The ASR rule *Block abuse of exploited vulnerable signed drivers* stops an app writing a known vulnerable driver to disk (recall *How EDR works*).
- **Detect.** A hardware-utility driver appearing on a machine that does not have that hardware, loaded from a user folder, with a new kernel driver service, is visible in Sysmon event 6 and System event 7045 (lesson 14).

The BYOVD timeline runs backwards from what patch management expects: the vendor's fix comes first and the attacks come later. A patch protects machines that run the vendor's software; it does nothing against an attacker who brings the vulnerable version. Only deny rules, by hash or by signer and version, close that gap.

blocks.question: Dell released fixed versions of its driver in May 2021. Why could Lazarus still abuse CVE-2021-21551 that autumn on a machine that may never have run Dell software?
options: Because the fix was not signed
Because Dell's fix only applied to Windows 7
Because the attackers brought the old, validly signed vulnerable driver themselves, and nothing on the machine denied that file
Because CISA had not yet listed the CVE
blocks.explain: BYOVD does not depend on the victim having the vulnerable software installed. The attacker drops the old file. A patch changes the vendor's software on machines that run it; a deny rule is needed to stop the old file loading anywhere.

blocks.question: Sophos reported that BlackByte removed kernel callbacks registered by security products. Which telemetry source is weakest for detecting what happens next?
options: A network sensor outside the host
The EDR sensor's own kernel callbacks on that host
Event 7045 recording the new driver service before the callbacks were removed
A cloud console alert that the sensor stopped reporting
blocks.explain: Once callbacks are removed, the sensor on that host stops receiving process, thread and image-load notifications, so it is the least reliable witness of later activity. Events written before the tampering, sensor health monitoring and off-host telemetry remain useful.

lessons.title: When the signing pipeline is the target: ADV220005

blocks.md: **Plain idea.** BYOVD abuses honest drivers with bugs. The 2022 case in this lesson is different: attackers got *their own malicious drivers* signed by Microsoft. If the signing service will sign your file, a signature tells defenders very little about intent. Tiny example: a Sysmon filter that ignores drivers "signed by Microsoft" would ignore these too.

blocks.title: ADV220005: from abused developer accounts to revocation

scenes.caption: Several Partner Center developer accounts submit malicious drivers and obtain Microsoft signatures, the same signatures honest vendors get.
On hosts where the attackers are already admin, the signed drivers load and are used after the break-in, for example before ransomware.
29 September 2022: another malicious submission is caught, and the sellers' accounts are suspended in early October.
19 October 2022: SentinelOne, Mandiant and Sophos report the activity to Microsoft, which investigates.
13 December 2022: Windows updates revoke the certificate for the affected files, Defender adds detections, and the recommended blocklist is updated.

blocks.md:
**Microsoft's response, from the advisory.** It released Windows security updates "revoking the certificate for impacted files", suspended the partners' seller accounts, and added blocking detections in Microsoft Defender (version 1.377.987.0 and newer) "to help protect customers from legitimately signed drivers that have been used maliciously in post-exploit activity". Updates were also made to the recommended driver blocklist, and "enabling Hypervisor-protected Code Integrity (HVCI) will automatically enforce the policy without needing to deploy the policy."

**Compare with AuKill** (from *How EDR works*): there the driver was a genuine, old Microsoft-signed Process Explorer driver abused for its features; here the drivers were malicious from the start. Both show that "signed by Microsoft" is a statement about the signing pipeline, not about the code.

**Defender takeaways.** Treat signer names as metadata, not trust. Allow by inventory (hashes or exact signer, file name and version of drivers you actually run). Alert on CodeIntegrity revocation events (3033, 3036, 3112). Keep Defender and the blocklist current, because the response arrived as signatures, revocations and blocklist entries.

blocks.code:
# Two ways to cut driver-load noise, tested on made-up loads.
loads = [
    {"name": "storport.sys", "signer": "Microsoft Windows", "sha256": "A1"},
    {"name": "netx.sys",     "signer": "Contoso HW",        "sha256": "B2"},
    {"name": "evil.sys",     "signer": "Microsoft HW Signing (toy)", "sha256": "C3"},
    {"name": "oldview.sys",  "signer": "Microsoft Corporation", "sha256": "D4"},
]
KNOWN_GOOD = {"A1", "B2"}            # hashes of drivers this fleet really runs
REVOKED_OR_BAD = {"C3", "D4"}        # from advisories and the blocklist

def keep_by_signer(e):               # like 'exclude if signature contains microsoft'
    return "microsoft" not in e["signer"].lower()

def keep_by_hash(e):                 # log everything not already known good
    return e["sha256"] not in KNOWN_GOOD

for rule in (keep_by_signer, keep_by_hash):
    logged = [e["name"] for e in loads if rule(e)]
    missed = [e["name"] for e in loads if e["sha256"] in REVOKED_OR_BAD and not rule(e)]
    print(f"{rule.__name__:15} logged={logged} missed_bad={missed}")

# Output:
# keep_by_signer  logged=['netx.sys'] missed_bad=['evil.sys', 'oldview.sys']
# keep_by_hash    logged=['evil.sys', 'oldview.sys'] missed_bad=[]
blocks.caption: Two noise filters for driver-load logging, tested on made-up events. Excluding by signer text, as in Sysmon's documented sample configuration, hides drivers that carry a Microsoft signature even when they are bad.

blocks.md: Every signature-based trust decision has an upstream: the people and processes that issue signatures. When that upstream is abused (stolen keys, fraudulent developer accounts), revocation, deny lists and inventory-based allowlists are what still work.

blocks.question: According to ADV220005, what had the attackers already achieved before they used the Microsoft-signed malicious drivers?
options: Administrative privileges on the compromised systems
Compromise of Microsoft's signing keys
A kernel exploit in Windows itself
Nothing: the drivers were the initial access vector
blocks.explain: The advisory says the attacker had already gained administrative privileges before using the drivers, and that Microsoft found no compromise of its own systems: the activity was limited to abuse of several developer program accounts.

blocks.question: Your Sysmon configuration excludes driver loads whose signature contains 'microsoft'. Which of these would you miss?
options: Only drivers signed by third-party vendors
Drivers whose signature status is Expired
Unsigned drivers
Malicious or vulnerable drivers carrying a Microsoft signature, such as the ADV220005 drivers or AuKill's old Process Explorer driver
blocks.explain: A signer-text exclusion trusts every file the signing pipeline produced. Both 2022 to 2023 cases involved Microsoft signatures. Excluding known-good hashes, or exact signer plus file name and version from your inventory, keeps the noise down without that blind spot.

lessons.title: The vulnerable driver blocklist: what it holds and how to deploy it

blocks.md: How it reaches machines: since the Windows 11 2022 update it is on by default for all devices and can be switched in the Windows Security app; it is also enforced (except on Windows Server 2016) whenever memory integrity, Smart App Control or S mode (a locked-down Windows mode that runs only Microsoft Store apps) is on. Microsoft updates it quarterly and ships it in monthly Windows updates. Vendors and researchers submit drivers through the Microsoft Security Intelligence driver submission page.

**The honest limits**, in Microsoft's words: blocking drivers "can cause devices or software to malfunction, and in rare cases, lead to blue screen"; the list "isn't guaranteed to block every driver found to have vulnerabilities"; and the downloadable version "usually contains a more complete set of known vulnerable drivers than the version in the OS", because Microsoft holds some blocks back while vendors move users to fixed versions. Already-running drivers stay loaded until a reboot.

**Inside the policy file.** The download is an App Control policy named *Microsoft Windows Driver Policy*. In the copy downloaded for this course (November 2026, version 10.0.29545.0) it contained two *Allow All* rules (so it only denies), about 1,700 hash deny rules, 160 file-attribute rules and 218 signer rules. Two rule shapes matter:
- **Deny by hash**: up to four Authenticode hashes per file (SHA-1, SHA-256 and the SHA-1 and SHA-256 hashes of the first page), so it matches however Windows validates the file. In this copy about a third of the hash rules are page hashes; many files carry only the two full hashes.
- **Deny by signer + file attribute**: a signing certificate plus an original file name and a version range, for example from 0.0.0.0 up to the last vulnerable version, so fixed versions from the same vendor still load.

blocks.title: A signer + name + version deny rule against ToyFan releases

scenes.caption: Six ToyFan releases, all signed by the same made-up Fabrikam certificate. Versions 1.0 to 1.4 have the SET_REG bug.
Rule: signer Fabrikam, OriginalFileName toyfan.sys, versions 0.0.0.0 to 1.4.0.65535. The vulnerable range is denied whatever its hash.
Version 1.5, the fix, is above the range and loads. A hash rule could not express that without listing every bad build.
Renaming 1.3 on disk to fan2.sys changes nothing: the rule reads OriginalFileName from the version resource inside the signed file, so it still matches.

blocks.code:
# A made-up blocklist in the shape of Microsoft's driver policy:
# deny by hash, or deny by signer + original file name + version range.
import hashlib
def h(s): return hashlib.sha256(s.encode()).hexdigest()[:12]   # short fake hashes

DENY_HASH = {h("toyfan 1.0 build"): "ToyFan 1.0"}
DENY_ATTR = [{"signer": "Fabrikam Code Signing", "orig": "toyfan.sys",
              "min": (0, 0, 0, 0), "max": (1, 4, 0, 65535)}]

def ver(s): return tuple(int(x) for x in s.split("."))

def verdict(d):
    if d["hash"] in DENY_HASH:
        return "BLOCK hash"
    for r in DENY_ATTR:
        if (d["signer"] == r["signer"] and d["orig"].lower() == r["orig"]
                and r["min"] <= ver(d["ver"]) <= r["max"]):
            return "BLOCK signer+name+version"
    return "allow"

S = "Fabrikam Code Signing"
loads = [  # disk name, OriginalFileName from the signed version resource
 {"disk": "toyfan.sys", "orig": "toyfan.sys", "ver": "1.0.0.0", "signer": S, "hash": h("toyfan 1.0 build")},
 {"disk": "toyfan.sys", "orig": "ToyFan.sys", "ver": "1.3.2.7", "signer": S, "hash": h("toyfan 1.3 build")},
 {"disk": "fan2.sys",   "orig": "toyfan.sys", "ver": "1.3.2.7", "signer": S, "hash": h("toyfan 1.3 build")},
 {"disk": "toyfan.sys", "orig": "toyfan.sys", "ver": "1.5.0.0", "signer": S, "hash": h("toyfan 1.5 fixed")},
]
for d in loads:
    print(f'{d["disk"]:11} {d["ver"]:8} {d["hash"]}  {verdict(d)}')
blocks.caption: A made-up blocklist with both rule shapes. The hashes are short fakes made from strings; real rules use full Authenticode hashes.

blocks.code:
toyfan.sys  1.0.0.0  fd5cf5bd76af  BLOCK hash
toyfan.sys  1.3.2.7  e51cdce06dde  BLOCK signer+name+version
fan2.sys    1.3.2.7  e51cdce06dde  BLOCK signer+name+version
toyfan.sys  1.5.0.0  d573d7412f85  allow
blocks.caption: Output of the script above (run with Python 3).

blocks.md:
**Deploying the fuller list** (Microsoft's steps): download the App Control policy refresh tool and the blocklist binaries; pick the *audit* or *enforced* version and rename it `SiPolicy.p7b`; copy it to `%windir%\system32\CodeIntegrity`; run the refresh tool. Verify with a **3099** event in `CodeIntegrity/Operational` whose policy name and ID match the policy. Microsoft's advice is to validate in **audit mode** first and read the audit block events before enforcing, and, if you merge it into an allowlist policy, to remove its *Allow All* rules first.

Pair it with the ASR rule *Block abuse of exploited vulnerable signed drivers*: Microsoft's page says the ASR rule stops an app *writing* a vulnerable signed driver to disk but "doesn't block a driver already existing on the system from loading", which the blocklist does.

The blocklist uses **Authenticode** hashes, which skip the signature and checksum fields of the file. Sysmon, most EDRs and threat-intel feeds use **flat file** hashes (SHA-256 of every byte). The two do not match for the same signed driver. Build each list with the hash type its consumer computes.

blocks.question: A deny rule in an App Control policy names a signer and OriginalFileName toyfan.sys with only MinimumFileVersion 1.4.0.0 set. According to Microsoft's rules page, which versions does it block?
options: Versions 1.4.0.0 and higher
Only version 1.4.0.0
Versions 1.4.0.0 and lower
All versions, because Deny ignores versions
blocks.explain: Microsoft documents that for Deny rules with only MinimumFileVersion, files with a version less than or equal to it are blocked; for Allow rules it is the opposite. It is easy to get backwards, which is why the downloadable blocklist usually states both a minimum (0.0.0.0) and a maximum.

blocks.question: After deploying the enforced blocklist with the refresh tool, a known vulnerable driver is still listed as running. What is the most likely reason?
options: The refresh tool failed silently
The blocklist only applies to new installations
Drivers that were already running stay loaded until the computer reboots
Memory integrity must be off for the blocklist to work
blocks.explain: Microsoft's page says running processes and drivers are not stopped when a new policy activates without a reboot. Check for the 3099 event to confirm the policy loaded, then reboot so the driver fails to load next time.

lessons.title: App Control driver policies: allow what you run, deny what you know

blocks.md:
**Plain idea.** The blocklist says "never these". An allowlist says "only these". Tiny example: a fleet of 500 laptops loads about 150 different drivers. If a policy allows exactly those drivers by publisher, file name and minimum version, then an attacker's old overclocking driver fails to load even if nobody has ever reported it as vulnerable. That is the step from lesson 10's known-bad list to a known-good list.

From *How EDR works* you know **App Control for Business** (formerly WDAC, Windows Defender Application Control), its audit events 3076 and enforce events 3077, and rolling out in audit first. This lesson covers what is specific to drivers. A useful detail from Microsoft's rules page: "By default, only kernel-mode binaries are restricted"; option **0 Enabled:UMCI** (user-mode code integrity) adds programs and scripts. So a **driver-only policy** is a natural first project: it touches far fewer files than an application allowlist.

**Rule options that matter for drivers**:
- **2 Required:WHQL**: "requires that every driver is WHQL signed and removes legacy driver support". This alone rejects old cross-signed drivers.
- **3 Enabled:Audit Mode**: log what would be blocked; remove it to enforce.
- **10 Enabled:Boot Audit on Failure**: if a boot-critical driver fails under enforcement, the policy drops to audit so Windows still starts.

**File rule levels for kernel code**: **WHQL** (anything Microsoft signed through WHQL), **WHQLPublisher** (plus the vendor's certificate name), **WHQLFilePublisher** (plus original file name and a minimum version), and **Hash** as the fallback. **FilePath** rules "can't be used to allow kernel mode drivers".

**Precedence**: App Control "first processes all explicit deny rules ... Then, it processes any explicit allow rules", then managed installer and ISG (Intelligent Security Graph, Microsoft's cloud reputation service) if enabled. Microsoft recommends separate ALLOW and DENY policies where supported, such as your allowlist beside its blocklist.

blocks.title: How a driver-only App Control policy decides

scenes.caption: A driver is about to load. The policy first looks for an explicit deny rule: a hash, or signer plus name plus version range.
ToyFan 1.3 matches the deny rule. Deny always wins, even though Fabrikam also appears in an allow rule. Enforced: block and log 3077.
netx.sys matches no deny rule, so the allow rules are checked: WHQLFilePublisher for Contoso, netx.sys, version 3.0 or higher. It loads.
An unlisted driver matches neither list. In an allowlist policy, no allow rule means no load. In audit mode it would load and log 3076 instead.

blocks.caption: A toy driver policy with Required:WHQL, one deny rule and one allow rule, run in audit and then enforce mode. Simplified: Windows also logs related events, such as 3089 with signature details and 3082 for a non-WHQL driver in audit.

blocks.code:
== audit mode
  netx.sys    load  
  toyfan.sys  load  3076 audit: would block (explicit deny)
  toyfan.sys  load  
  oldtool.sys load  3076 audit: would block (not WHQL signed)
== enforced
  netx.sys    load  
  toyfan.sys  BLOCK 3077 enforced (explicit deny)
  toyfan.sys  load  
  oldtool.sys BLOCK 3077 enforced (not WHQL signed)
blocks.caption: Output of the script above (run with Python 3).

              FileName="toyfan.sys" MinimumFileVersion="0.0.0.0"

</FileRules>
