blocks.md: Build the driver allowlist from reality: scan a set of reference machines, generate WHQLFilePublisher rules with a hash fallback, deploy in audit, and read every 3076 for a few weeks. Each 3076 is either a driver you forgot (add it) or one you never wanted (investigate it).

blocks.question: A driver-only policy (no Enabled:UMCI) is enforced. A user runs an unsigned script and an unsigned EXE. What happens?
options: Both are blocked, because App Control blocks all unsigned code
Neither is restricted by this policy, because without UMCI only kernel-mode binaries are checked
The EXE is blocked and the script runs
Both run but generate 3077 events
blocks.explain: Microsoft's rule options table says policies restrict only kernel-mode binaries by default; option 0 Enabled:UMCI extends checks to user-mode executables and scripts. A driver-only policy is narrower but much easier to deploy.

blocks.question: Your allowlist trusts Fabrikam drivers at WHQLPublisher level. Microsoft's blocklist, deployed as a second policy, denies Fabrikam toyfan.sys up to 1.4. Will ToyFan 1.3 load?
options: No, because a file must pass every active policy and explicit deny rules are processed first
Yes, because the allow rule names the publisher
Yes, because the blocklist contains Allow All rules
It depends on the order the policies were deployed
blocks.explain: With multiple policies, a file must be allowed by each of them. The blocklist policy denies ToyFan 1.3; its Allow All rules only mean it does not restrict anything else. Within any one policy, explicit deny rules take precedence over allow rules.

lessons.title: VBS and memory integrity: taking code checks out of the kernel

blocks.md: **Plain idea.** Every check so far runs in the kernel. But BYOVD gives an attacker kernel-level powers, and code in the kernel can, in principle, undo checks made by other code in the kernel. The fix is to move the most important checks somewhere the kernel cannot reach. Tiny example: a guard who works inside the building can be bribed by anyone who gets inside; a guard behind bulletproof glass, who controls the doors, cannot.

**VBS** (virtualization-based security) "uses hardware virtualization and the Windows hypervisor to create an isolated virtual environment that becomes the root of trust of the OS that assumes the kernel can be compromised." The **hypervisor** is the thin layer below the operating system that controls the CPU's virtualization features. It builds on **VSM** (Virtual Secure Mode), which splits the machine into **VTLs** (virtual trust levels): "VTL0 is the least privileged level", where the normal NT kernel, drivers and apps run, and VTL1 is more privileged; "currently, only two VTLs are implemented." Each VTL has its own memory access protections, managed by the hypervisor in a way "system level software running in the partition" cannot modify.

scenes.caption: Without VBS, apps, the NT kernel and every driver share the kernel's power. A BYOVD driver sits at the same level as the code that checks drivers.
With VBS, the hypervisor runs below Windows and owns the second-level address translation (SLAT) tables that decide what physical memory each VTL may read, write or execute.
Memory integrity (HVCI) moves kernel-mode code integrity into VTL1. The NT kernel asks; VTL1 checks the signature and policy, then asks the hypervisor to make the pages executable.
A BYOVD driver in VTL0 can still write VTL0 data, but it cannot reach VTL1 memory or rewrite the hypervisor's page permissions. Its kernel power stops at the VTL line.

blocks.md:
**What memory integrity enforces.** Microsoft: kernel memory pages "are only made executable after passing code integrity checks inside the secure runtime environment, and executable pages themselves are never writable. That way, even if there are vulnerabilities like a buffer overflow that allow malware to attempt to modify memory, executable code pages cannot be modified, and modified memory cannot be made executable." This is W^X (write xor execute) from *Exploit mitigations*, enforced by the hypervisor for the kernel. On supported versions it also enforces the vulnerable driver blocklist.

**Requirements and defaults.** VBS needs a 64-bit CPU with virtualization extensions and SLAT, an IOMMU (input-output memory management unit, which confines devices' DMA, direct memory access), a TPM 2.0 (Trusted Platform Module, a key-storing chip) and Secure Boot (firmware runs only signed boot code). Memory integrity "works better" with Intel MBEC or AMD GMET; older CPUs emulate it more slowly. It is on by default on many new Windows 11 PCs; Windows Security warns when it is off.

blocks.title: Kernel page permissions with memory integrity off, then on

scenes.caption: Four kernel pages: driver code (read and execute), driver data and a pool buffer (read and write), and a buffer an attacker filled with code.
Memory integrity off: kernel code holding BYOVD powers asks to make the attacker's buffer RWX. The kernel's own page tables allow it.
Memory integrity on: the same request is refused. Execute rights come only from VTL1 after a code integrity check, and never together with write.
Patching driver code is refused too: code pages stay RX. But data pages remain writable, which is the gap Kernel Data Protection (next lesson) narrows.

blocks.code:
# Toy model of memory integrity: a "secure" checker (VTL1) owns the
# execute permission of kernel pages; the normal kernel (VTL0) cannot grant it.
pages = {"drv_code": "RX", "drv_data": "RW", "pool_buf": "RW"}
APPROVED = {"drv_code"}                    # passed the code integrity check

def vtl0_set(page, perm, hvci):
    if hvci and "X" in perm and (page not in APPROVED or "W" in perm):
        return f"{page}: refused {perm} (hypervisor keeps W^X, CI-approved only)"
    pages[page] = perm
    return f"{page}: now {perm}"

for hvci in (False, True):
    pages.update(drv_code="RX", drv_data="RW", pool_buf="RW")
    print("== memory integrity", "ON" if hvci else "OFF")
    print(" ", vtl0_set("pool_buf", "RWX", hvci))   # make injected bytes runnable
    print(" ", vtl0_set("drv_code", "RWX", hvci))   # patch existing code
    print(" ", vtl0_set("drv_data", "RW", hvci))    # ordinary data write: allowed

# Output:
# == memory integrity OFF
#   pool_buf: now RWX
#   drv_code: now RWX
#   drv_data: now RW
# == memory integrity ON
#   pool_buf: refused RWX (hypervisor keeps W^X, CI-approved only)
#   drv_code: refused RWX (hypervisor keeps W^X, CI-approved only)
#   drv_data: now RW
blocks.caption: A toy model of the W^X rule memory integrity enforces. Simplified: the real check happens in VTL1 and the hypervisor's SLAT tables, not in a Python dict.

blocks.md:
**Operating it.** Turn it on in Windows Security (Device security, Core isolation, Memory integrity), Intune, Group Policy (*Turn on Virtualization Based Security*) or the registry. Check it with `Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_DeviceGuard -Namespace root\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard`: a 2 in **SecurityServicesRunning** means memory integrity is running, and **VirtualizationBasedSecurityStatus** 2 means VBS is enabled and running. Two hardening switches: **UEFI lock** stops it being turned off remotely (you then need firmware access), and **Mandatory** makes the loader refuse to boot if the hypervisor or secure kernel fails to load.

The cost is compatibility: "Some applications and hardware device drivers may be incompatible with memory integrity," which "in rare cases may result in a boot failure". Pilot on test groups first.

Memory integrity protects kernel **code**, not kernel **data**. A BYOVD driver that lets a caller change kernel memory can still alter data structures in VTL0, such as callback registrations or policy variables, and memory integrity does not stop that. HVCI is necessary, not sufficient.

blocks.question: With memory integrity on, an attacker uses a vulnerable driver's write IOCTL to copy code into a kernel pool buffer and then tries to run it. What stops them?
options: The driver's signature check
PatchGuard
Nothing: HVCI only protects user mode
The hypervisor refuses to make the page executable, because execute rights come only from VTL1 after a code integrity check
blocks.explain: Under memory integrity, kernel pages become executable only after passing code integrity checks in VTL1, and executable pages are never writable. Writing code into data memory does not make it runnable.

blocks.question: Win32_DeviceGuard shows VirtualizationBasedSecurityStatus = 2 but SecurityServicesRunning does not contain 2. What is true?
options: Memory integrity is running but VBS is not
VBS is running but memory integrity is not
Both are running
Neither is enabled
blocks.explain: VirtualizationBasedSecurityStatus 2 means VBS is enabled and running. SecurityServicesRunning lists the services in use, and the value 2 means memory integrity. VBS can run with other services (such as Credential Guard) without memory integrity.

lessons.title: Kernel Data Protection and PatchGuard: guarding data, catching patches

blocks.md: **Plain idea.** Memory integrity locks kernel code. Two more mechanisms address the rest. **Kernel Data Protection** (KDP) locks chosen *data* so even kernel code cannot change it. **Kernel Patch Protection** (KPP), informally called PatchGuard, *notices* when key kernel code or structures were changed and stops the machine. One prevents, the other detects after the fact. Tiny example: a variable that says "code integrity policy: enforce" is worth protecting with KDP; a modified system service table is the kind of change KPP reports.

**KDP.** Announced by Microsoft in July 2020 to address attackers who, after code integrity and Control Flow Guard, turn to data corruption, KDP lets a driver mark memory read-only for the whole OS using VBS. The WDK documents the static form, `MmProtectDriverSection`, which "read-only protects a section of a loaded driver by using the services provided by the Virtual Secure Mode (VSM)": it "protects the physical memory backing the driver's section using the SLAT table ... managed by the VSM. The protected memory will be made read-only for the entire Operating System," and "there is no way to remove the protection" unless the driver opted in to unloading. If VSM is off, the call fails with `STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_STATE`. A dynamic form allocates read-only memory from a secure pool.

Microsoft's examples include code integrity policy state, protected so that a signed but vulnerable driver cannot change the policy and then load unsigned code.

**KPP (PatchGuard).** Scott Field, a Windows kernel security architect at Microsoft, described it in 2006: first supported on x64 editions of Windows Server 2003 SP1 and Windows XP Professional x64, it "monitors if key resources used by the kernel or kernel code itself has been modified. If the operating system detects an unauthorized patch of certain data structures or code it will initiate a shut down of the system." It applies to Microsoft products too: "No code is allowed to modify the kernel using unsupported patching techniques."

The shutdown appears as **bug check 0x109, CRITICAL_STRUCTURE_CORRUPTION**, whose fourth parameter names what changed: for example 0x1 *a function modification*, 0x2 *the interrupt dispatch table (IDT)*, 0x7 *a critical MSR modification*, 0xA *modification of a system service function*, 0x1C *driver object corruption*. Field was clear about the limit: KPP "does not prevent all viruses, rootkits, or other malware... It helps prevent one way to attack the system: patching kernel structures and code."

blocks.code:
# Toy contrast: KDP prevents a write to protected data; a KPP-style check
# only notices a change later and stops the machine. (Simplified models.)
import hashlib
memory = {"ci_policy": b"enforce=1", "service_table": b"open,read,write"}
kdp_protected = {"ci_policy"}                       # made read-only via VTL1

def write(region, value):
    if region in kdp_protected:
        return f"write to {region}: blocked by the hypervisor (KDP)"
    memory[region] = value
    return f"write to {region}: succeeded"

def snapshot(region):
    return hashlib.sha256(memory[region]).hexdigest()[:8]

baseline = snapshot("service_table")              # taken when the system boots
print(write("ci_policy", b"enforce=0"))
print(write("service_table", b"open,HOOK,write"))           # a hook patched in
now = snapshot("service_table")
print("integrity check:", baseline, "vs", now)
if now != baseline:
    print("bug check 0x109 CRITICAL_STRUCTURE_CORRUPTION (machine stops)")

# Output:
# write to ci_policy: blocked by the hypervisor (KDP)
# write to service_table: succeeded
# integrity check: f54522f1 vs fb2af542
# bug check 0x109 CRITICAL_STRUCTURE_CORRUPTION (machine stops)
blocks.caption: A toy contrast between prevention (KDP) and after-the-fact detection (a KPP-style check). Simplified: the real mechanisms work very differently inside; only the outcomes are modelled.

blocks.title: Which defence covers which BYOVD step (simplified)

scenes.caption: Rows are defences, columns are attacker steps. 1 means the defence prevents the step, 0.5 means it detects it or covers it only partly, 0 means it does not apply. A summary judgement from this course's sources.
No single row is full. The ASR rule and the blocklist only know listed drivers; an inventory allowlist also stops unlisted ones at load time.
Once a driver is loaded, HVCI protects code, KDP protects chosen data, and PatchGuard can only catch some changes afterwards. Ordinary kernel data stays exposed.
Detection touches the early steps and is what tells you an attack happened at all. Layer prevention at the load step, because after it the options narrow quickly.

blocks.md: Misconception: "PatchGuard makes kernel tampering impossible." Microsoft's own description is narrower: it detects certain modifications and shuts the system down, and it does not prevent all malware. In the BlackByte case, Sophos reported that security callbacks were removed regardless. Treat KPP as a tripwire, not a wall.

blocks.question: A security vendor's driver keeps its configuration in a data section and wants even a compromised kernel to be unable to change it after start-up. Which mechanism fits?
options: PatchGuard
An App Control deny rule
Kernel Data Protection with MmProtectDriverSection
The ASR rule for vulnerable drivers
blocks.explain: MmProtectDriverSection makes a driver's data section read-only for the whole OS through VSM and SLAT, and the protection cannot be removed. PatchGuard only detects changes to certain structures and does not protect a vendor's own data.

blocks.question: A server crashes with bug check 0x109 and parameter 4 equal to 0xA. What does Microsoft's documentation say happened?
options: Modification of a system service function was detected
A driver read memory out of bounds
The vulnerable driver blocklist blocked a driver
Memory integrity found an incompatible driver
blocks.explain: Bug check 0x109 means the kernel detected critical code or data corruption; parameter 4 value 0xA is 'Modification of a system service function'. Microsoft lists three general causes: a driver modifying kernel code or data, a breakpoint set without a debugger attached at boot, or hardware memory corruption.

lessons.title: Seeing driver loads: Sysmon 6, CodeIntegrity, 7045 and callbacks

blocks.md: **Plain idea.** Every BYOVD attack has to load a driver, and loading a driver is noisy if you are listening in the right places. Tiny example: one malicious load can leave a *service installed* record, a *driver loaded* record with hashes and signer, and, if a policy objected, a *blocked* or *would have blocked* record, all within a second.

The sources, from the prereq courses and Microsoft's documentation:
- **System event 7045**: a service was installed; for drivers the service type reads *kernel mode driver* (*Windows for security*).
- **Sysmon event 6, Driver loaded**: "information about a driver being loaded on the system. The configured hashes are provided as well as signature information. The signature is created asynchronously for performance reasons and indicates if the file was removed after loading." Fields include `ImageLoaded`, `Hashes`, `Signed`, `Signature` and `SignatureStatus`. Hashes can be SHA1 (the default), MD5, SHA256 or IMPHASH.
- **CodeIntegrity/Operational** (an ETW channel, like every modern event log): 3001 an unsigned driver tried to load, 3004 an invalid signature (for example not WHQL where WHQL is required), 3033, 3036 and 3112 for revocations, 3076 and 3077 for policy audit and block, 3089 with signature details, 3099 for a policy load, 3111 for a file that did not meet the HVCI policy.

blocks.title: One driver load and the records it leaves

scenes.caption: An admin (or attacker) creates a kernel driver service. The Service Control Manager records System event 7045 with the service type 'kernel mode driver'.
Starting the service asks the kernel to load the .sys file. Code integrity checks signature and policy first.
If a policy objects, CodeIntegrity logs 3077 (enforced block) or 3076 (audit), each with a 3089 holding signature details, and the load fails or goes ahead.
If it loads, the kernel runs image-load notify routines. For a driver, the routine's ProcessId is zero. Sysmon's driver turns this into event 6.

blocks.md:
**What to look for in each record.**
- **Where it was loaded from.** Drivers normally live under `System32\drivers` or the driver store. A driver loaded from a user profile, `Temp` or `ProgramData` is unusual.
- **Who signed it, and is the signature still good?** `SignatureStatus` other than *Valid* (for example *Expired* or *Revoked*) deserves a look, but remember from lesson 9 that a valid Microsoft signature is no proof of innocence.
- **Is it in your inventory?** A hardware-utility driver on a machine without that hardware is a strong signal.
- **Is its hash known bad?** Match Sysmon's flat-file hashes against intelligence that uses flat-file hashes, not against the Authenticode hashes in App Control policies (lesson 10).
- **What happened around it?** A new 7045, a 3077 a second earlier for a *different* driver (the attacker trying again), and a sensor that stops reporting minutes later tell a story no single event tells.
EDR sensors see the same moment through the image-load notify routine from *How EDR works*: Microsoft documents that its `ProcessId` "is zero if the newly loaded image is a driver."

blocks.code:
# Triage synthetic Sysmon event 6 (driver loaded) records.
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
EV = """<Events>
<Event><EventData><Data Name="ImageLoaded">C:\\Windows\\System32\\drivers\\netx.sys</Data>
<Data Name="Hashes">SHA1=C3,SHA256=AA11</Data><Data Name="Signature">Contoso HW</Data>
<Data Name="SignatureStatus">Valid</Data></EventData></Event>
<Event><EventData><Data Name="ImageLoaded">C:\\Users\\kim\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\fan2.sys</Data>
<Data Name="Hashes">SHA1=D4,SHA256=BB22</Data><Data Name="Signature">Fabrikam Code Signing</Data>
<Data Name="SignatureStatus">Valid</Data></EventData></Event>
</Events>"""
KNOWN_BAD_SHA256 = {"BB22"}       # flat-file hashes, made up
INVENTORY = {"netx.sys"}          # drivers this fleet is expected to load

for ev in ET.fromstring(EV).iter("Event"):
    f = {d.get("Name"): d.text for d in ev.iter("Data")}
    sha = dict(x.split("=") for x in f["Hashes"].split(","))["SHA256"]
    path = f["ImageLoaded"].lower(); name = path.split("\\")[-1]
    why = []
    if sha in KNOWN_BAD_SHA256: why.append("hash on blocklist")
    if f["SignatureStatus"] != "Valid": why.append("signature not valid")
    if "\\temp\\" in path or "\\users\\" in path: why.append("user-writable path")
    if name not in INVENTORY: why.append("not in inventory")
    print(name, "|", f["Signature"], "|", ", ".join(why) or "expected")
blocks.caption: Triage synthetic Sysmon event 6 records with four checks: known-bad hash, signature status, user-writable path and inventory. Every value is made up.

blocks.code:
netx.sys | Contoso HW | expected
fan2.sys | Fabrikam Code Signing | hash on blocklist, user-writable path, not in inventory
blocks.caption: Output of the script above (run with Python 3).

blocks.md: Sysmon's documented sample configuration excludes driver loads whose signature contains 'microsoft' or 'windows'. It keeps the log small and, as lesson 9 showed, hides Microsoft-signed abuse. Exclude by known-good hash or exact inventory instead, and test your filter against the cases in this course.

blocks.question: A Sysmon event 6 shows SignatureStatus 'Valid' for a driver loaded from a user's Temp folder, and the host has no matching hardware. Which reading is best?
options: Suspicious: valid signatures are exactly what BYOVD drivers carry, and the path and missing hardware are anomalies
Benign, because the signature is valid
A Sysmon bug, because drivers cannot load from Temp
Benign, because Sysmon would mark a vulnerable driver as Revoked
blocks.explain: BYOVD relies on valid signatures, so the signature status alone clears nothing. Drivers can load from any path an admin chooses. Sysmon reports signature validity, not vulnerability, so a vulnerable driver shows as Valid unless its certificate was revoked.

blocks.question: You want to correlate a CodeIntegrity 3077 block event with the signature details of the blocked file. What links them?
options: The process ID
The file's flat SHA-256 hash
The event record number plus one
The Correlation ActivityID in the System portion of the events
blocks.explain: Microsoft documents that 3089 signature events are correlated with 3004, 3033, 3034, 3076 and 3077 events and can be matched using the Correlation ActivityID in the System portion of the event. One 3089 is written for each signature on the file.

lessons.title: Detection as code for drivers: Sigma rules, tests and conversion

blocks.md:
**Plain idea.** From *Logging and detection engineering* you know **Sigma**: one YAML rule format that tools convert into each SIEM's query language. Driver loads fit it well. Sigma's Windows log sources include the category `driver_load` (Sysmon event 6 and equivalent EDR data) and the service `codeintegrity-operational`. The public SigmaHQ rule set already has rules for both: for example *Driver Load From A Temporary Directory* (Florian Roth of Nextron Systems, 2017, level high, with the honest note that there is "a relevant set of false positives depending on applications in the environment"), and *CodeIntegrity - Blocked Image/Driver Load For Policy Violation* matching event 3077.

Here we write a rule, convert it with **pySigma**, the Python library behind Sigma's converters, and measure how noisy each idea is on a synthetic fleet.

blocks.code:
# Convert a driver-load Sigma rule to a Splunk search with pySigma.
from sigma.collection import SigmaCollection
from sigma.backends.splunk import SplunkBackend
from sigma.pipelines.sysmon import sysmon_pipeline
from sigma.pipelines.splunk import splunk_windows_pipeline

RULE = r"""
title: Driver Loaded From A User-Writable Folder Or Without A Valid Signature
id: 6f1d2c1e-0000-4000-8000-000000000001
status: experimental
logsource:
    product: windows
    category: driver_load
detection:
    user_path:
        ImageLoaded|contains:
            - '\Users\'
            - '\Temp\'
    valid_sig:
        SignatureStatus: 'Valid'
    condition: user_path or not valid_sig
falsepositives:
    - Driver installers that unpack to a temporary folder
level: high
"""
pipeline = sysmon_pipeline() + splunk_windows_pipeline()
backend = SplunkBackend(processing_pipeline=pipeline)
print(backend.convert(SigmaCollection.from_yaml(RULE))[0])
blocks.caption: A driver-load rule converted to Splunk SPL with pySigma 2.1.1, the Splunk backend and the Sysmon pipeline, installed in a virtual environment. The output is the real converter output.

blocks.code: source="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventCode=6 (ImageLoaded IN ("*\\Users\\*", "*\\Temp\\*") OR NOT SignatureStatus="Valid")
blocks.caption: Output of the script above (run with Python 3).

blocks.code:
title: CodeIntegrity Blocked Or Revoked Driver
logsource:
    product: windows
    service: codeintegrity-operational
detection:
    selection:
        EventID:
            - 3077   # blocked by an enforced App Control policy
            - 3033   # failed policy, often a revoked signature
            - 3036   # certificate revoked by the issuing authority
    condition: selection
level: high

# Converted with the same backend and the Splunk Windows pipeline:
# source="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational" (EventCode IN (3077, 3033, 3036))
blocks.caption: A second rule on the CodeIntegrity log. The conversion line is the real output of pySigma for this rule (the id, status and author fields are omitted here for space).

blocks.code:
# Alert volume of four driver-load rules on a synthetic week (500 hosts).
import random
random.seed(7)
INVENTORY = {"netx.sys", "gpu.sys", "storport.sys", "wifi.sys", "vpn.sys"}
BLOCKLIST = {"fan2.sys"}                 # stands in for a hash list
loads = []
for host in range(500):
    for d in random.sample(sorted(INVENTORY), 4):           # normal boot loads
        loads.append({"name": d, "path": "system32", "status": "Valid"})
    if random.random() < 0.04:                              # vendor updater
        loads.append({"name": "vendorupd.sys", "path": "temp", "status": "Valid"})
    if random.random() < 0.10:                              # new webcam driver
        loads.append({"name": "newcam.sys", "path": "system32", "status": "Valid"})
loads.append({"name": "fan2.sys", "path": "temp", "status": "Valid", "bad": True})
loads.append({"name": "oldtool.sys", "path": "programdata", "status": "Expired", "bad": True})

rules = {
    "every driver load": lambda e: True,
    "not in inventory": lambda e: e["name"] not in INVENTORY,
    "user path or bad sig": lambda e: e["path"] != "system32" or e["status"] != "Valid",
    "hash on blocklist": lambda e: e["name"] in BLOCKLIST,
}
for name, rule in rules.items():
    hits = [e for e in loads if rule(e)]
    tp = sum(1 for e in hits if e.get("bad"))
    print(f"{name:21} alerts={len(hits):5}  true positives={tp}")

blocks.title: Precision and recall of four driver-load rules (synthetic week)

scenes.caption: Precision: the share of alerts that were real. Alerting on every driver load gives 2 true alerts out of 2085, about 0.1 percent: the base-rate trap from the logging course.
Recall: the share of bad loads caught. The hash rule is perfectly precise but caught only 1 of 2, because the second driver was not on the list yet.
So run more than one: a precise hash or blocklist rule that pages someone, and a broader path, signature and inventory rule that feeds a daily review queue.

blocks.md:
**Testing and tuning, the detection-as-code way.**
- Keep synthetic events like the ones in this course as **test fixtures**: one that must fire (driver from `Temp`, *Expired* signature) and one that must not (an inventoried driver from `System32\drivers`).
- Put the **inventory** in a lookup table the rule joins against, not in the rule itself, so adding a new webcam driver is a data change.
- Map rules to ATT&CK: T1068 for BYOVD, and [T1685](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1685/) *Disable or Modify Tools* for what usually follows.
- Expect hash lists to lag: in the synthetic week the second bad driver was not on the list yet. That is why the broader rule exists.

Sigma's rule format is documented at [sigmahq.io](https://sigmahq.io/docs/basics/rules.html) and pySigma at [its GitHub repository](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/pySigma).

Driver detection works best in layers of precision: an exact-match rule (known-bad hashes, CodeIntegrity blocks and revocations) that pages, and an anomaly rule (unusual path, bad signature status, not in inventory) that someone reviews daily.

blocks.question: The 'hash on blocklist' rule had 100 percent precision but missed one of the two bad drivers. What does that tell you?
options: The rule is broken and should be deleted
Exact-match rules only catch what is already known; they need a broader companion rule for new or unlisted drivers
Precision and recall always move together
The second driver must have been signed by Microsoft
blocks.explain: A list catches only listed items, so its recall depends on how current the list is. Pairing it with a broader anomaly rule (path, signature, inventory) trades precision for recall, and a review queue absorbs the extra alerts.

blocks.question: Why convert Sigma rules with a pipeline such as the Sysmon pipeline rather than only a backend?
options: Pipelines make the rule run faster
Backends cannot handle the contains modifier
The pipeline maps the generic log source (category driver_load) to the concrete source and event ID, such as Sysmon's Operational log and EventCode 6
Pipelines encrypt the query
blocks.explain: A Sigma rule says driver_load, which is generic. In the conversion above, the Sysmon pipeline turned driver_load into Sysmon event ID 6, and the Splunk Windows pipeline mapped that to the Sysmon Operational source and EventCode=6. Without the pipelines the query would search every source for those field names.

lessons.title: Responding to a BYOVD alert, and the cost of kernel code

blocks.md: **Plain idea.** A BYOVD alert means two things at once: someone has admin rights they should not have, and your sensor on that host may already be blind. Tiny example: at 10:05 a driver loads from `Temp`; at 10:05:30 the EDR heartbeat stops. Anything the sensor reports after that is suspect, so you act on the host from outside it.

A response plan, in the usual order of confirm, contain, scope, eradicate and recover:
1. **Confirm.** Get the driver's hashes (flat and, if you can, Authenticode), signer, version and original file name. Is it on Microsoft's blocklist, in CISA's KEV catalog, in vendor advisories?
2. **Contain from outside.** Use network isolation that does not depend on the possibly tampered sensor, for example switch or firewall controls, and disable the admin account that was used.
3. **Scope.** Search the SIEM for the same flat hash, the same service name and the same path pattern on every host. BYOVD is rarely the first step, so look for how admin rights were gained.
4. **Eradicate.** Remove the driver service and file, then **reboot**: a running driver stays loaded until restart, even after a blocklist update.
5. **Recover and harden.** Reset exposed credentials, confirm the sensor reports again, turn on what was missing (memory integrity, blocklist, ASR rule, App Control driver rules), and report a newly abused driver to its vendor and to Microsoft's driver submission page.

blocks.title: A BYOVD incident on one host (synthetic)

scenes.caption: Minutes after 10:00. An admin shell runs an installer from Downloads, creates a driver service, and the first driver is blocked by policy (3077).
The attacker retries with a different driver at 10:05. It loads (Sysmon 6) and 26 seconds later the EDR sensor stops reporting.
The correlated score crosses the threshold. The responder isolates the host from the network side and disables the admin account used.
Scoping and eradication follow: fleet-wide hash search, service and file removal, reboot, then hardening. The clock for the rest of the fleet starts at the first 3077.

blocks.code:
# Join synthetic events from three logs into one host timeline, then score it.
events = [
 ("10:02:11", "Security 4688",   "admin shell runs installer.exe from Downloads"),
 ("10:02:40", "System 7045",     "service 'fansvc' installed, type: kernel mode driver"),
 ("10:02:41", "CodeIntegrity 3077", "fan2.sys blocked: violated code integrity policy"),
 ("10:05:03", "System 7045",     "service 'fansvc2' installed, type: kernel mode driver"),
 ("10:05:04", "Sysmon 6",        "fan9.sys loaded from ...\\Temp\\, signer Tailspin"),
 ("10:05:30", "EDR heartbeat",   "sensor stopped reporting"),
]
SCORE = {"7045": 2, "3077": 3, "6": 2, "heartbeat": 5}
total = 0
for t, src, msg in sorted(events):
    pts = next((v for k, v in SCORE.items() if src.endswith(k)), 0)
    total += pts
    print(f"{t}  {src:19} +{pts}  {msg}")
print("score", total, "action:", "isolate host" if total >= 8 else "review")
blocks.caption: Joining synthetic events from three logs into one host timeline with a simple score. Real SOCs do this with correlation rules; the weights here are illustrative.

blocks.md:
**The cost of kernel code, for defenders too.** Every defence in this course runs in or next to the kernel, and the kernel punishes mistakes. Microsoft warns that blocking drivers can, rarely, cause a blue screen, and that memory integrity can make incompatible drivers fail at boot. The CrowdStrike outage of 19 July 2024 (*How EDR works*, and [CISA's alert](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2024/07/19/widespread-it-outage-due-crowdstrike-update)) showed a security product's kernel component taking machines down at scale. The lesson is the same on both sides: stage changes, start in audit, use canary groups, keep a recovery path (Windows RE, the Windows Recovery Environment, and access to firmware settings if you use UEFI lock).

And the first item of Microsoft's driver checklist applies to security tools as much as to fan utilities: confirm that a kernel driver is required at all. Microsoft's Windows Resiliency Initiative, from the EDR course, is moving antivirus and endpoint protection towards user mode for exactly this reason.

**Practise legally.** Work only on machines you own or are authorised to test.
- Read the IOCTL sample in Microsoft's [Windows-driver-samples](https://github.com/microsoft/Windows-driver-samples) repository: note which Access bits its control codes declare and how its device is secured, then write down how you would tighten it.
- In a Windows VM you own: turn on memory integrity, deploy the blocklist in audit mode, and read the CodeIntegrity log (3099, 3076); install Sysmon and watch event 6 for your own drivers.
- Write and test Sigma rules for `driver_load` and `codeintegrity-operational` with [pySigma](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/pySigma) and the synthetic events from this course.
- Blue-team investigation practice: [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/) and [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/).

BYOVD response starts from two assumptions: the attacker is already admin, and the host's sensor may be blind. Contain from outside the host, scope by hash and service name across the fleet, reboot to unload, and fix the gap that let the driver load.

blocks.question: After removing a malicious driver's service and file, and updating the blocklist, why is a reboot part of eradication?
options: To rotate the BitLocker key
Because a driver that is already loaded stays in kernel memory until restart; removing the file and adding blocks does not unload it
Because Sysmon only logs after a reboot
Because the blocklist only works in Safe Mode
blocks.explain: Microsoft's blocklist page notes that already running drivers the policy would block keep running until the computer restarts. Deleting the file does not unmap the code from kernel memory either.

blocks.question: Which containment step is most reliable when the alert says the EDR sensor on the host stopped reporting after a suspicious driver load?
options: Ask the EDR agent on the host to isolate it
Run a full antivirus scan on the host
Wait for the sensor to come back
Isolate the host with network controls outside it, such as the switch port or firewall, and disable the admin account used
blocks.explain: If a BYOVD driver blinded the sensor, commands sent through that sensor may not work or may not be honest. Controls outside the host do not depend on its integrity, and disabling the compromised admin account cuts the attacker's access elsewhere.
